opus-5.5.text:
Well, simulated annealing is an idea that comes from computer science, and it turns out to be a really nice way of thinking about a fundamental tension that any intelligent system faces, which is the tension between exploration and exploitation.

Imagine you're trying to find the best solution to a problem, and you can picture all the possible solutions as a kind of landscape, with peaks and valleys. If you just start out by looking locally, going to whatever is a little bit better than where you are now, you're likely to get stuck on a local peak. You'll find something that's pretty good, but you'll miss the much higher mountain that's just over the horizon.

What simulated annealing suggests is that you start out with a very "hot" search. You bounce around the space very widely and fairly randomly, trying out all sorts of possibilities, including ones that look unlikely or even worse than what you've got. Then, gradually, you "cool off." You narrow in, become more focused, and start exploiting what you've learned to fine-tune the solution.

What's striking is that childhood looks like nature's way of implementing exactly that strategy. Children are the hot search. They're noisy, variable, and random. They try out all sorts of wild hypotheses, and from an adult's point of view that looks like being bad at things. But that's exactly what you want in the early exploratory phase. In our experiments, preschoolers will sometimes come up with an unusual hypothesis that adults just won't consider, because the adults have already cooled down and settled on the more obvious answer.

Scientists are interesting because they're adults who have institutionalized a bit of that childlike heat. Science is a protected space where you're allowed to be wrong, play around, and entertain crazy ideas, but it also has the cooling mechanisms of peer review, replication, and testing. So you might say science combines the child's exploration with the adult's exploitation. The difference is that for children, the heat comes for free; it's built into their biology and their protected period of immaturity. Scientists have to work hard to recapture it, and our institutions have to support them in doing that.

r001.rationale: Describes starting with a hot, wide, random search and gradually cooling into a focused search that refines the solution.

r002.rationale: Calls children the hot search and says they try wild hypotheses and many possibilities.

r003.rationale: Says science combines children's exploration with adult exploitation, including speculative play and later peer review, replication, and testing.

r004.rationale: Mentions unusual hypotheses adults may overlook, but does not say major scientific paradigm shifts often originate in improbable ideas.

r005.rationale: Does not discuss grant proposals or say their absence lets children sustain exploration.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, simulated annealing is this idea from computer science, from optimization, that if you're trying to search through a big space of possibilities, there's a tradeoff between exploring widely and exploiting what you already know. And the trick is that you start out at a high "temperature," where the system is very noisy, very random, jumping around all over the place, and then you gradually lower the temperature, so the system settles into a solution. If you start out cool, you get stuck in a local optimum. If you stay hot forever, you never settle on anything useful.

And it struck me that this is a really good way of thinking about childhood. Children are the high-temperature phase of the human search algorithm. They're noisy, they're variable, they try things that look crazy from the adult point of view, and that's precisely what lets them find solutions that a more focused, exploitative adult would never stumble on. Adults are the low-temperature phase. We're much better at actually getting things done, at exploiting the knowledge we've got, but we're much worse at generating genuinely new hypotheses. So the long human childhood, which is otherwise a bit of an evolutionary puzzle, looks like a solution to the explore-exploit tradeoff: you have one part of the lifespan that's dedicated to exploration and another part that's dedicated to exploitation.

Now, the connection to scientists is that science, as an institution, is trying to do something similar, but it's doing it socially rather than developmentally. An individual scientist is mostly a cooled-down adult who has invested in a particular picture of the world. So what you need is some way of injecting temperature back into the system. You get that partly through young scientists, graduate students, people who haven't yet committed to the paradigm, and partly through things like play and basic research, where you're deliberately not optimizing for a payoff. One of the things we've found in our lab is that children will actually explore more when the evidence is confusing or ambiguous, and when there's no obvious reward on the table, and I think that's exactly the regime good science needs.

The difference is that children do it effortlessly and involuntarily, because their brains are built for it, their prefrontal cortex isn't yet in charge, whereas scientists have to do it on purpose, against the grain of their own cognition. So in a way the question for a scientific community, or for any institution that wants to discover things, is: how do you keep some of that childlike high temperature around without losing the ability to actually settle on an answer? That's hard, and I don't think we're very good at it.

r001.rationale: It describes starting at high temperature with noisy, random exploration, then lowering the temperature so the search settles into a solution.

r002.rationale: It explicitly calls children the high-temperature phase of the human search algorithm and describes their variable, wide-ranging exploration.

r003.rationale: It says science needs to reintroduce exploration while retaining the ability to settle on answers, but does not clearly state that scientists must alternate between speculative exploration and refining existing ideas.

r004.rationale: It does not say that major scientific paradigm shifts often begin with ideas that seem improbable.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss grant-proposal obligations or connect their absence to children's unconstrained exploration.

astra-6.text:
Well, simulated annealing gives us a useful way of thinking about the trade-off between exploration and exploitation. If you’re searching for a good solution, you don’t want to just keep making small improvements to whatever you’re already doing. You can get stuck at a local optimum—something that’s better than the nearby alternatives but much worse than something farther away.

So you start with a high-temperature search, where you try lots of different possibilities, including possibilities that initially look worse. Then you gradually cool down and concentrate on making the best solution work.

I think childhood is something like that high-temperature period. Children are willing to entertain unlikely hypotheses and try things that an adult would dismiss. And they can do that partly because they’re protected: Someone else is making sure that they get fed and that they don’t wander into traffic. Adults have to actually get things done, which tends to favor a more focused search.

Scientists have a related problem. They need periods when they can play with ideas without knowing whether those ideas will lead anywhere, and periods when they rigorously test and develop a particular idea. So the analogy isn’t simply that children explore and scientists don’t. It’s that science needs to preserve some of that childhood openness while also having the discipline to settle on, and evaluate, a solution.

r001.rationale: It describes a high-temperature search over many possibilities, including worse ones, followed by cooling and concentrating on the best solution.

r002.rationale: It compares childhood to a high-temperature period in which children entertain unlikely hypotheses and try possibilities adults might dismiss.

r003.rationale: It says science needs periods of playing with ideas and periods of rigorously testing and developing a particular idea.

r004.rationale: It mentions unlikely hypotheses and speculative scientific ideas, but does not say that major scientific paradigm shifts often originate in improbable ideas.

r005.rationale: It says children are protected and adults must get things done, but does not mention grant-proposal obligations as the reason for children's unconstrained exploration.

sol-6.1.text:
The idea behind simulated annealing is that if you’re trying to find the best solution to a problem, you don’t want to just keep making small improvements to the solution you already have. You can get stuck on a local optimum. So you start out with a high temperature, where you’re willing to try a lot of different possibilities, even possibilities that look worse. Then you gradually cool down and settle on a solution.

I think childhood is something like that high-temperature period. Children are willing to consider unlikely hypotheses, try things that don’t seem very sensible, and explore without knowing what the payoff will be. Adults are much better at taking what we’ve already learned and using it to get things done, but that can make it harder for us to move away from our existing ideas.

Scientists have to do both. You need periods when you’re playing with possibilities, entertaining crazy ideas, and then periods when you’re testing carefully and working out the details. One of the interesting things about science is that it creates room for adults to do some of that characteristically childlike exploration.

r001.rationale: Describes trying many possibilities, including ones that seem worse, then cooling down and settling on a solution.

r002.rationale: Explicitly compares childhood to the high-temperature phase and describes children trying unlikely hypotheses and exploring possibilities.

r003.rationale: Says scientists need periods of speculative play followed by careful testing and working out details.

r004.rationale: Does not say that major scientific paradigm shifts often begin with improbable ideas.

r005.rationale: Does not mention grant proposals or connect their absence to children's unconstrained exploration.
